name: Didymus the Blind
knownFor: A blind teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, who answered the Arians, admired Origen, and taught Jerome of Strido and Rufinus of Aquileia.
dates: Died aged 85, by Palladius's account. Jerome, writing his Lives of Illustrious Men, says he was still living and "has already passed his eighty-third year."

keyWorks.title: On the Trinity, three books
keyWorks.about: Socrates names three books on the Trinity; the Library holds the Greek text Mingarelli printed in 1769 from one manuscript, as Didymus's

keyWorks.title: On the Holy Spirit
keyWorks.about: which Jerome of Strido says he translated into Latin; Jerome's Latin is not held in this Library

keyWorks.title: Commentaries on Origen's First Principles
keyWorks.about: which Socrates says defended Origen; not held

traces: Rufinus of Aquileia says he became teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, approved by Athanasius, and that he himself heard him speak.
Jerome of Strido studied with him at Alexandria and called him master: "for what I did not know I learned from him, and what I knew already I did not forget."
remembered: Socrates of Constantinople says he was then regarded as "the great bulwark of the true faith" against the Arians.
Sozomen says many came to Alexandria "for the express purpose of hearing, or, at least, of seeing him."
Evagrius Scholasticus, writing in the sixth century, reports that the emperor Justinian condemned Origen, Didymus and Evagrius.

uncertain: The story of Antony and Didymus is told by four writers with differences. Jerome of Strido has Antony speak of "ants and flies and gnats", Socrates of Constantinople of "gnats and flies", Sozomen of "rats, mice, and the lowest animals", and Rufinus of Aquileia of mice, flies and lizards. Sozomen gives it as what "is related", and Socrates as what "is said".
His years are not fixed. Palladius says he died at 85. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Jerome gives about 311 to 396. Blomfield Jackson's note to Theodoret gives about 309 to 399.
His praise of Origen is known from Socrates, who quotes it. The commentaries Socrates names are not held.
Sozomen reports, as what "is said", that he learned his letters from carved tablets felt with his fingers.
Evagrius Scholasticus names the three condemned men but gives no year in the passage.
